items.followUp: Define reduction and give one way it can occur.

rubric.description: Defines oxidation as loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of oxidation.

rubric.description: Defines reduction as gain of electrons, loss of oxygen, or gain of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any one correct definition of reduction.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, or loss of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, loss of oxygen, or gain of hydrogen.

items.followUp: What is the role of mitosis in growth and repair?

rubric.why: Identifies the process that produces new cells.
rubric.description: States that mitosis produces new cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying mitosis or cell division.

rubric.description: Explains that mitosis replaces or repairs lost or damaged cells/parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking mitosis to replacement, repair, or regeneration.

modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells.
These cells replace lost or damaged cells and help regenerate body parts.

items.followUp: Write the classification of a cat from kingdom to species.

rubric.why: These are the higher taxonomic groups in human classification.
rubric.description: Gives the human kingdom, phylum, class, and order.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct higher groups: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, and Primates.

rubric.why: These complete the classification to species.
rubric.description: Gives the human family, genus, and species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct lower groups: Hominidae, Homo, and sapiens.

modelAnswer: Kingdom: Animalia
Phylum: Chordata
Class: Mammalia
Order: Primates
Family: Hominidae
Genus: Homo
Species: Homo sapiens

items.followUp: What is taxonomy, and what additional relationships does systematics study?

rubric.why: Defines the main work of taxonomy.
rubric.description: States that taxonomy deals with identification, nomenclature, and/or classification of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing taxonomy as identification, naming, or classification.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the broader scope of systematics.
rubric.description: States that systematics studies organismal diversity and evolutionary relationships; taxonomy is part of this broader study.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the evolutionary or broader relationship aspect of systematics.

modelAnswer: Taxonomy deals with the identification, naming, and classification of organisms.
Systematics is broader: it studies organismal diversity and their evolutionary relationships, and includes taxonomy.

items.followUp: Differentiate between a reactant and a product in a chemical reaction.

rubric.why: Identifies what a substrate is in an enzyme reaction.
rubric.description: Defines a substrate as the substance on which an enzyme acts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the substrate is the reactant acted upon by an enzyme.

rubric.why: Identifies what is made by the reaction.
rubric.description: Defines products as the substances formed by the enzyme-catalysed reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that products are formed in the reaction.

modelAnswer: A substrate is the reactant on which an enzyme acts.
Products are the substances formed by the enzyme-catalysed reaction.

items.followUp: Name the two categories of enzymes based on where they act, and define each.

rubric.why: Identifies enzymes that act within cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for intracellular enzymes or enzymes working inside cells.

rubric.why: Identifies enzymes that act outside cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for extracellular enzymes or enzymes working outside cells.

modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes work inside the cells in which they are produced.
Extracellular enzymes are released from cells and work outside them.

items.followUp: Explain how the lock-and-key model accounts for enzyme specificity.

rubric.why: Describes the specific fit between enzyme and substrate.
rubric.description: States that the substrate fits the enzyme's active site because their shapes are complementary.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the specific lock-and-key fit.

rubric.why: Describes the outcome of binding in the model.
rubric.description: States that an enzyme-substrate complex forms and products are released while the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complex or product-release outcome.

modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, an enzyme's active site has a specific shape complementary to its substrate, like a lock fits its key.
The substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex; products are released and the enzyme remains unchanged.

items.followUp: Why are minerals important for the normal functioning of organisms?

rubric.description: States that minerals are inorganic substances or elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying minerals as inorganic.

rubric.description: States that minerals are needed for normal growth, development, or functioning.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct role or requirement.

modelAnswer: Minerals are inorganic elements or substances required by organisms in small quantities.
They are essential for normal growth, development, and functioning.
